title: Awareness / Spontaneity / Intimacy
setting: Saturday afternoon. Amar and Leela, friends since college, are out running errands together with no particular agenda - a market stall, a walk, then coffee.

L1.line: Here, try a slice. Isn't it just like the ones we used to get from that cart near college?
cues: inviting a comparison to the past
an actual orange in your hand, right now
L1.question: Which of the three capacities of autonomy is actually being tested when Amar decides how to answer this?

options.text: Awareness - whether he actually tastes and notices this orange, or just repeats the expected comparison.
options.feedback: Right. Berne's awareness means seeing, hearing, and tasting what's actually in front of you in your own way, not the way you were taught to - the test here is whether Amar checks the orange or just checks the memory.

options.text: Spontaneity - whether he picks an unusual response.
options.feedback: Spontaneity is about freedom of feeling and expression, not novelty for its own sake - this moment is specifically about direct sensory contact with something real, which is awareness.

options.text: Intimacy - whether he's honest with Leela.
options.feedback: Not yet - nothing vulnerable has been shared here for Amar to meet candidly. This is a much smaller moment: just noticing what's true about an orange.

L1.lesson: Autonomy's three capacities aren't interchangeable. Awareness is the specific capacity for direct, unfiltered contact with what's actually here - the easiest way to lose it is to answer from the stored script ("just like the old days") instead of your own senses.

L2.intro: Three small moments across the afternoon. Each one offers Amar a scripted, easy response and a real one.

beats.line: Here, try a slice. Isn't it just like the ones we used to get from that cart near college?
cues: the actual orange is right here

options.text: Actually - this one's way more tart than I remember. Really good, though.
options.outcome: Leela laughs. "Huh, didn't expect that answer." She tries one too, actually paying attention this time.
options.lesson: Noticing what's actually true now, even when it contradicts the expected memory, is Berne's awareness: direct contact with the present instead of fitting experience to an old script.

options.outcome: Automatic. Leela shrugs and moves on to the next stall.
options.lesson: A polite, reflexive match isn't wrong, but it's autopilot - agreeing with the expected comparison instead of actually checking it against what's in your mouth.

options.text: Oh my god, remember that one time at the cart when-
options.outcome: Leela's attention drifts halfway through; the orange goes unfinished in Amar's hand.
options.lesson: This swaps the actual orange for a stored story about oranges - the present moment becomes a prop for an old narrative instead of something tasted.

beats.line: You're always so calm about everything. Doesn't anything ever actually get to you?
cues: needling a role you always play
inviting the performance of your usual steady self

options.text: Actually, yeah - that thing in the meeting Thursday really got under my skin.
options.outcome: "Oh! Okay, wasn't expecting that." A real moment opens up between them.
options.lesson: Spontaneity is freedom to feel and express whatever actually fits right now, not being locked into one rehearsed role - dropping "the calm one" for the honest reaction is the autonomous move.

options.text: Ha, nothing really fazes me, you know that.
options.outcome: Predictable. Leela nods like she expected exactly that - the conversation stays exactly where it's always been.
options.lesson: This is the opposite of spontaneity: the rehearsed, on-brand reply that keeps the relationship right where the script says it should stay.

options.outcome: Leela blinks, stung. "...Okay, sorry I asked." She backs off.
options.lesson: A snap reaction can feel spontaneous, but it's just as automatic as the calm deflection - real spontaneity is choosing freely among the feelings available, not firing off whichever one is loaded.

beats.line: Honestly... I've been kind of lonely since I moved here. I don't even know why I'm telling you this.
cues: nothing attached, no ask, no angle

options.text: Thanks for telling me. I felt kind of the same way my first year here - want to grab lunch this week, just the two of us?
options.outcome: Leela's shoulders drop. "...Yeah. I'd really like that." Plans get made, real ones.
options.lesson: Berne's intimacy is candid, game-free exchange with no ulterior transaction - meeting vulnerability with vulnerability, plus something concrete, instead of managing it from a distance.

options.text: You'll make friends soon, don't worry about it!
options.outcome: "...Yeah, maybe." Kind, but Leela goes a little quiet after.
options.lesson: Reassurance from Parent is well-meant, but it answers from above instead of meeting her where she actually is - it's comfort, not the candid exchange intimacy actually calls for.

options.text: Oh, you should totally come to this thing I'm hosting next week, everyone will love you!
options.outcome: Leela smiles, but something in her face closes down. "...Sure, maybe."
options.lesson: Turning her candid moment into a pitch swaps real exchange for a performance - a disguised invitation standing in for the much smaller, much realer thing she actually needed, which was just to be heard.

fields.label: In under 50 words: name Berne's three components of autonomy and give one moment from today (real or imagined) for each.
In one sentence: spontaneity is often confused with impulsiveness. What's actually the difference?

echo.setting: The next evening, a voice note from Leela.
echo.line: "Hey - thanks again for lunch plans. Also, random, but your coffee order is somehow always the most predictable thing about you."
echo.shape: same three-beat shape as L2, lighter stakes
